title: Follow the Moon’s “Wrinkles”! A “Coat” Theory Emerges
part1:
Almost no one looks up at the Moon and thinks, “It’s dressed warmly again tonight.” But a study of the “wrinkles” on the Moon’s surface has raised the possibility that a kind of “coat” makes it harder for heat inside the Moon to escape. A study of wrinkles has somehow turned into a clothing check. What is going on?

First, let’s look at the wrinkles themselves. They are cliffs that are steep on one side and gentle on the other. They are thought to have formed when the ground was squeezed together and the rock on one side rose up over the rock on the other. With clothes, you’d reach for an iron, but here we’re talking about rock. These wrinkles are on a very different scale.
part2:
The research team used images from a probe’s camera to map these cliffs. Based on their distribution, the team estimated that the Moon’s radius had shrunk by about 42 to 46 meters. They did not wrap a huge tape measure around the Moon. Instead, they read the amount of “size adjustment” from the changes left in the ground.

But don’t rush to conclude, “The Moon has shrunk by about that much since it was born!” This figure is an estimate of shrinkage during a later period in the Moon’s history, recorded by a relatively young fault. What’s more, it is not yet clear when that fault began to form. The wrinkles have a mystery about their age, too.

Meanwhile, some models that calculate how the Moon cools predict that its total shrinkage would be greater than this estimate. You might want to ask, “Were the calculations wrong?” But wait before deciding. The periods being compared and the ways they were studied are different. Simply putting the numbers side by side does not settle the question.
part3:
One clue that may help explain the difference is a thick layer of broken rock. What matters is not only that the rock is broken, but also that there are gaps in the layer. If this layer acted like insulation, it may have kept heat from escaping and slowed the Moon’s cooling and shrinking.

Rough rocks might act like warm clothing. It is hard to tell just by looking. When we think of putting on extra clothes on a cold day or adding insulation to a house, the Moon’s distant heat history suddenly feels much closer. Of course, the Moon is not actually wearing clothes.

Still, it has not been shown that the “coat” is the cause. It is only one possible explanation. The Moon’s wrinkles are clues not only to “How much has it shrunk?” but also to “How quickly has it been giving off heat?” Next time you look at the Moon, try to imagine the “coat” hidden beneath its patterns. You may see the Moon a little differently.
in_one_line: Mapping the Moon’s wrinkles suggests its radius shrank by about 42 to 46 meters during a later period in its history. The wrinkles may help reveal how quickly the Moon lost heat, and a thick layer of porous rock may have slowed its cooling like insulation.
